subject: physiology
title: Heart Sounds, Jugular Venous Pulse, and Frank-Starling Law

steps.tx: Auscultation of the precordium reveals acoustic vibrations generated by abrupt deceleration of blood and closure of heart valves. The **first heart sound** (S1) marks the onset of ventricular systole, produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, best heard at the cardiac apex with a low-pitched lub duration of zero point one four seconds.
steps.say: The first heart sound marks the onset of systole, caused by closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves, heard best at the cardiac apex.

rows: Low-pitched dull thud; physiological in youth

steps.tx: The **second heart sound** (S2) marks the end of ventricular systole and the onset of diastole, produced by closure of the aortic and pulmonary semilunar valves. S2 is shorter, crisper, and higher pitched than S1, best appreciated at the second right and left intercostal spaces along the sternal border.
steps.say: The second heart sound marks the onset of diastole, caused by closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves, heard best at the base of the heart.

right.title: Pulmonary Component (P2)
points: Lower pressure (15 mmHg in pulmonary artery)
Softer and normally confined to second left intercostal space
Delayed during inspiration, creating physiological splitting

steps.tx: During inspiration, negative intrathoracic pressure increases venous return to the right heart, prolonging right ventricular ejection and delaying pulmonary valve closure. Concurrently, pulmonary vascular capacitance expands, reducing left heart filling and accelerating aortic closure. This separation of A2 and P2 by forty to fifty milliseconds defines normal **physiological splitting** of S2.
steps.say: Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart, delaying pulmonary valve closure and creating physiological splitting of the second sound.

steps.tx: Pathological heart sounds arise during diastolic filling. A **third heart sound** (S3) occurs during the rapid filling phase, produced as blood rushes into a dilated, volume-overloaded ventricle, causing ventricular wall tensing (ventricular gallop). S3 is normal in children and pregnancy but indicates heart failure or severe mitral regurgitation in older adults.
steps.say: The third heart sound occurs during rapid ventricular filling in volume-overloaded dilated ventricles, typical of systolic heart failure.

steps.tx: A **fourth heart sound** (S4) occurs in late diastole, generated when vigorous atrial contraction forces blood into a stiff, non-compliant, hypertrophied ventricle (atrial gallop). S4 is always pathological, heard in concentric left ventricular hypertrophy from hypertension or severe aortic stenosis, and is absent in atrial fibrillation because coordinated atrial contraction is lost.
steps.say: The fourth heart sound is produced by atrial contraction into a stiff, non-compliant ventricle, typical of hypertensive hypertrophy, and absent in atrial fibrillation.

left.title: Third Heart Sound (S3 Gallop)
points: Occurs in early diastole during rapid filling phase
Associated with ventricular volume overload and dilation
Low ejection fraction and systolic heart failure

right.title: Fourth Heart Sound (S4 Gallop)
points: Occurs in late diastole during active atrial kick
Associated with ventricular stiffness and pressure hypertrophy
Preserved ejection fraction and diastolic dysfunction

steps.tx: Right atrial pressure fluctuations transmit retrograde into the internal jugular vein, forming the **jugular venous pulse**. The JVP waveform features three positive peaks (a, c, and v) and two negative descents (x and y). The a wave represents active atrial contraction, the c wave reflects tricuspid bulging during isovolumetric contraction, and the v wave reflects atrial venous filling.
steps.say: The jugular venous pulse displays three positive waves: a wave from atrial contraction, c wave from tricuspid bulging, and v wave from venous filling.

rows: Cannon a waves in complete AV block; absent in AF

Tricuspid valve bulging during isovolumetric systole
Passive venous filling of right atrium against closed tricuspid
Giant systolic cv waves in tricuspid regurgitation
Rapid emptying of right atrium following tricuspid opening
Blunted in cardiac tamponade; steep in constrictive pericarditis

steps.tx: The volume of blood ejected by each ventricle during a single heartbeat is the stroke volume, normally seventy millilitres. Dividing stroke volume by end-diastolic volume yields the **ejection fraction**, a crucial index of left ventricular contractile performance. Normal ejection fraction ranges between fifty-five and seventy percent, depressed below forty percent in systolic heart failure.
steps.say: Ejection fraction is stroke volume divided by end-diastolic volume, normally 55 to 70 percent, declining below 40 percent in systolic failure.

nodes.label: Stroke Volume = EDV - ESV = 70 mL Ejected

steps.tx: The heart matches its output to its filling with no instructions from the brain. The **Frank Starling law** states that greater end diastolic stretch produces a stronger contraction, because sarcomeres lengthen toward their optimal overlap and calcium sensitivity rises. This keeps right and left outputs equal beat by beat. A failing ventricle operates on a flattened curve, where extra filling buys pressure and congestion rather than flow.
steps.say: Frank Starling law matches contraction strength to diastolic stretch, balancing both ventricles. The failing heart flattens that curve.

vis.caption: A rising curve links ventricular filling to stroke volume, flattened in failure. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: The intrinsic ability of the heart to adapt its stroke volume to varying venous filling is formulated by the **Frank-Starling law**. Within physiological limits, the force of ventricular contraction is directly proportional to the initial resting length of the cardiac myocytes. Increased venous return stretches myocytes, optimizing cross-bridge overlap and increasing troponin C calcium sensitivity to augment stroke volume.
steps.say: The Frank-Starling law states that greater venous filling stretches myocytes, increasing cross-bridge overlap and stroke volume to balance biventricular output.
